bridge: O01 introduced files and folders. Practise in your own named lab folder, using harmless files that you can recreate.
teaching:
### Locate yourself before running a command

The current working directory is the folder from which a command starts. A relative path starts there. An absolute path starts at the filesystem root. A filename that works in one folder may point nowhere in another.

Use the shell's command for showing the current directory and listing files. Change into the practice folder and list it again. Check the result rather than assuming a command succeeded.

### Read a command in parts

A command has a program name and arguments. Options adjust its behaviour. Quoting can keep spaces or special characters inside one argument. Without suitable quoting, the shell may split a filename or interpret characters as instructions.

The shell and the program are separate interpreters. A character can have meaning to the shell before the program ever receives it.

### Learn from the help text

Use the command's help or manual page to check its supported options. Identify what it reads, what it changes and how it reports failure. Command versions and platforms can differ.

### Inspect before changing files

Start with listing and reading operations. Before a write, move or deletion, identify the exact target and check that it belongs to the disposable lab. Do not paste an unexplained command with elevated privileges. In this course, being able to explain the target and effect is part of completing the task.
example:
mkdir -p cyber-shell/copies
cd cyber-shell
pwd
printf 'hello\n' > 'first note.txt'
cp 'first note.txt' copies/backup.txt
ls -l
cat copies/backup.txt
# Expected content: hello
explanation: mkdir creates only the named practice tree. The redirection > writes printf output to a file and replaces existing contents at that path, so choose a fresh directory. cp creates an independent copy. After cd copies, cat ../"first note.txt" reaches the original through the parent directory. Record the actual pwd output rather than assuming every machine uses the same home path.
exercise: In your fresh learning folder, run the example one command per line. Predict which command creates a directory, which writes a file and which makes an independent copy. Then run cd copies, pwd, and cat ../"first note.txt". Finally run cd .. and pwd again. Write the two different directory paths and both displayed file contents. If cd fails, use pwd and ls to check where you are; do not add administrator privileges to fix a path mistake.
solution: From copies, cd .. returns to cyber-shell. Both displayed files contain hello. The absolute pwd path ends in the expected directory. A command written cd ... normally names a literal directory called ... and is not parent traversal.
challenge: Without the example, create a folder named second lab containing a text file and a copies subfolder. Copy the file, access it using a relative path from copies, and explain which command changes future relative-path resolution.
challenge_solution: Correct quoting keeps second lab as one path. cd changes the working directory. A reproducible answer includes the directory tree and actual read-back contents, not just successful exit status.
